title: How Rolex makes Money
fullText: Rolex makes around $14 billion a year, and it does it while refusing to sell you a watch. Here's a test you can run today. Walk into a Rolex showroom with $20,000 in cash. Point at a steel Daytona, the racing chronograph that's been on the wrist of half of Hollywood. At the counter, it lists for around $16,900. So, the money is not the problem. Say you want it right now at full price, they'll turn you down. Not because it's sold out. It might be sitting there behind the glass. They'll put your name on the list and tell you to wait years on a good day. That is not a broken shop. That is the most valuable watch company on Earth doing exactly what it means to do. One in every three luxury Swiss watches sold anywhere is a Rolex. And the harder Rolex is to buy, the more people want it. So, how does a company get rich? By turning paying customers away. The answer isn't really about watches at all. It comes down to one thing Rolex has spent 100red years building. And I'll show you exactly what it is by the end. Starting with the strangest clue. Nobody owns Rolex. You can't buy shares in it. There's no founder cashing out. No investors demanding a bigger payday every year. When the man who built it, Hans Wilsdorf, died, he left the whole company to a foundation he had set up. That foundation still owns all of it today. And a large share of the profits reportedly goes through charitable and social causes in Geneva rather than into any private owner's pocket. Think about what that does. A normal luxury brand lives under constant pressure to sell more and grow faster because their shareholders want their return. The foundation doesn't need Rolex to grow. It needs Rolex to stay Rolex. That is a quiet superpower. It lets Rolex do things that would get a normal boss fired. It can make fewer watches than it is able to. It can leave money on the table this year to protect the name in 30 years. It can watch you walk out empty-handed and know your disappointment just made the brand stronger. Most companies exist to make as much profit as possible. Rolex exists to make as much desire as possible and the profit follows. Which leaves a strange question. If Rolex doesn't even need the money, why make its watches so impossible to get? For years, people told themselves a simple story. Rolexes are hard to buy because Rolex can't make enough of them. Each one is lovingly handmade. Demand is just too high. That story is mostly a myth. Rolex makes around 1.1 million watches a year. It is one of the most automated, most industrialized watch makers in Switzerland. with the factories and the money to make far more. It chooses not to. Once you see it as a choice, everything flips. Rolex isn't failing to keep up with demand. It's carefully keeping demand a step ahead of supply. When there is always one more person who wants a watch than there are watches to sell. The waiting list becomes the advertising. People don't just want the watch, they want to be the kind of person who was allowed to get one. Walk into that showroom as a stranger and you'll feel it. The watches everyone wants. the steel Submariner at around $10,000. The red and blue GMT Master 2 collect his nickname, the Pepsi. The Daytona are almost never just sitting there for anyone to buy. To get one, it helps enormously to already be a known customer and someone who has bought from that dealer before. So, people start buying the watches. They can get an Oyster Perpetual at around $6,000, a Datejust at around $8,000. the ones nobody's waiting for, hoping it earns them a place in line for the one they actually want. You spend the money to earn the right to spend more money. Rolex never has to say any of this out loud. The scarcity does the talking and it quietly turns buying a watch into a game you have to qualify for. The line isn't a flaw in the system. The line is the product. And that scarcity does one more thing. The thing that built an entire second market Rolex didn't create, doesn't sell in, and somehow completely controls. The moment you finally walk out with that watch on your wrist, it's already worth more than you paid. Normally, once you sell something, what the buyer does with it is their business. If they flip it for a profit, that profit is theirs. For most of Rolex's history, that's exactly what happened. The same steel Daytona listed at around $16,900 has traded secondhand for roughly double north of $30,000. And the Pepsi GMT has sold for well over twice its sticker price. People bought Rolexes not to wear but to flip. A whole industry of dealers lived in the gap between what Rolex charged and what the world would pay. Look at what that gap does to the brand. Every time a Rolex changes hands for more than it costs new, it sends a message. This isn't a watch. It's an asset. It holds its value. It might even make you money. Push that idea to its limit and you get the Daytona once worn by the actor and racing driver Paul Newman, which sold at an auction in 2017 for $17.8 million. That reputation is worth more than any advert Rolex could buy. And for decades, Rolex got it for free. Free wasn't enough. Billions of dollars were moving through a market Rolex never touched. So, Rolex moved in. It started certifying used watches, stamping its own name onto the secondhand trade, and taking a cut of the trust it had built. Then, it did something that stunned the industry. Rolex bought Buckler, one of the biggest luxury watch retailers on the planet. In a single move, the company that only made watches could now control how they were sold and resold at the counter. The last part of the game it didn't hold was suddenly in its hands. So, here's where it gets sharper. Rolex now controls the price going in and the price coming out. And what it does with that control breaks a rule you were taught your whole life. It raises prices almost every year quietly right across the range. For most products, charging more means selling less. For Rolex, it barely moves the queue. A higher price doesn't scare off buyers. It reassures them. It makes the watch a stronger symbol, not a worse deal. Rolex is one of the only companies on earth that can lift its prices again and again and watch demand hold or even grow. That pricing power is why it sits alone at the top, taking around a third of the entire Swiss watch market by itself. More than the next several brands combined. When one company controls that much and answers to no shareholders, it doesn't follow the industry. The industry follows it. But pricing power like that needs one more thing underneath it. And it's the part most people never think about. To command your price, you first have to command your cost. Most brands you can name are really just assemblers. They design something, buy the part from suppliers, bolt it together, and add a logo. Their profit is whatever is left between what the suppliers charge and what the customers pay. Rolex barely plays that game. It makes almost everything itself. It runs its own foundry and casts its own gold. It makes its own steel cases, its own movements, its own tiny internal parts, all under its own roof. Very few companies on Earth control this much of their own product. And when you own the whole chain from raw metal to finished watch, your costs are yours to command. That is a big part of how a watch costing a fraction of its price to build can sell for what it does. Then there's the half you actually see. Rolex spends a fortune putting its crown everywhere that signals success. The most prestigious tournaments in tennis and golf, explorers, champions, record-breakers. It sells the watch as proof that you've arrived. So follow the loop. Rolex makes its own parts and controls the costs. It limits supply to keep demand hungry. It spends heavily to tie the crown to status and a foundation shields it from ever breaking those rules for a quick payday. Every piece protects the others and all of it rests on one thing. It's fragile. It took more than a century to build and it is the real product Rolex sells. It's never the watch. So where did it come from? None of this belief existed by accident. Rolex built it one stunt at a time. In the 1920s, a wristwatch was seen as fragile and a little feminine. Serious men carried pocket watches. Wilsorf bet the company on changing that. In 1926, Rolex built the first properly waterproof wristwatch case and called it the Oyster. Then he needed the world to believe it. So in 1927, when a young typist named Mercedes Gita swam the English Channel, Rolex strapped an oyster to her wrist for the crossing. It came out of the freezing water still ticking. Rolex bought the front page of a newspaper to announce it in one of the first celebrity endorsements in history and it worked. From then on, the playbook never changed. Put the watch wherever people do the impossible. When the first climbers reached the summit of Everest in 1952, Rolex watches went with them and the model built for that kind of expedition became the explorer. When a submarine touched the deepest point in the ocean, an experimental Rolex were strapped to the outside and it came back working. The ancestors of today's sea dweller and deep sea racing drivers, deep sea divers, pilots, polar expeditions, everyone became a story, and every story said the same thing. This watch belongs on the wrist of someone extraordinary. By the time you were born, the work was done. The crown didn't need to explain itself anymore. It simply meant success in a way almost everyone on earth already quietly agreed on. That shared belief built over decades and impossible to buy overnight is the real thing standing behind every waiting list and every price tag. Strip it all back. Rolex is not in the business of telling time. Your phone does that for free and it does it better. What Rolex sells is belief. The belief shared by millions of people who have never met that a small object on your wrist means something, that it signals success and taste, that it will still be worth something in 30 years, that it says you made it without you saying a word. That belief is the most valuable thing Rolex owns, and everything it does protects it. The no at the counter, the controlled supply, the resale value, the foundation that guards it from short-term greed. For more than a hundred years, Rolex has turned steel and oil into meaning. And meaning has almost unlimited margins. That's how Rolex really makes money. Not by selling watches, but by building desire, guarding it at every step and refusing to ever let it run out. So the next time you see one behind the glass, and you notice the price, and you wonder why anyone would wait years for something a phone does better, remember what you're really looking at. Not a watch. The most successful desire machine in the history of retail, owned by no one, answering to no one. Getting richer every year by telling paying customers no. And maybe the real question isn't why a Rolex costs what it costs. It's how many other things you want someone else taught you to want. segments.text: Not by selling watches, but by building desire, guarding it at every step and
segments.viText: Không phải bằng cách bán đồng hồ, mà bằng cách xây dựng niềm khao khát, bảo vệ nó ở mọi bước đi và

segments.text: refusing to ever let it run out.
segments.viText: từ chối không bao giờ để nó cạn kiệt.

segments.text: So the next time you see one behind the glass, and you notice the
segments.viText: Vì vậy, lần tới khi bạn nhìn thấy một cái đằng sau tấm kính, và bạn nhận thấy

segments.text: price, and you wonder why anyone would wait years for something a phone does
segments.viText: giá, và bạn thắc mắc tại sao mọi người lại chờ đợi hàng năm trời để có được một tính năng mà một chiếc điện thoại có thể làm được

segments.text: better, remember what you're really looking at.
segments.viText: tốt hơn hết, hãy nhớ những gì bạn thực sự đang nhìn vào.

segments.text: Not a watch.
segments.viText: Không phải là một chiếc đồng hồ.

segments.text: The most successful desire machine in the history of retail, owned by no one,
segments.viText: Cỗ máy khao khát thành công nhất trong lịch sử bán lẻ, không thuộc sở hữu của ai,

segments.text: answering to no one.
segments.viText: không trả lời ai cả.

segments.text: Getting richer every year by telling paying customers no.
segments.viText: Trở nên giàu có hơn mỗi năm bằng cách nói không với những khách hàng trả tiền.

segments.text: And maybe the real question isn't why a Rolex costs what it costs.
segments.viText: Và có lẽ câu hỏi thực sự không phải là tại sao một chiếc Rolex lại có giá như vậy.

segments.text: It's how many other things you want someone else taught you to want.
segments.viText: Quan trọng là bạn muốn có bao nhiêu thứ khác mà người khác đã dạy bạn muốn.

segments.text: If this one surprised you, a like and a subscribe would be much appreciated.
segments.viText: Nếu điều này làm bạn ngạc nhiên, một lượt thích và một lượt đăng ký sẽ được đánh giá cao.

segments.text: We'll see you in the next video.
segments.viText: Chúng tôi sẽ gặp bạn trong video tiếp theo.

segments.text: Bye-bye.
segments.viText: Tạm biệt.
